name: Jōmon & Yayoi Periods
intro: Japan's earliest inhabitants left behind remarkable pottery, sophisticated hunter-gatherer societies, and the agricultural foundations upon which all later civilisations would be built. The transition from Jōmon to Yayoi is one of the most consequential transformations in Japanese prehistory.

sections.body:
The Jōmon period (c. 14,000–300 BCE) takes its name from the characteristic cord-marked (jōmon) patterns pressed into clay pottery — some of the oldest fired ceramics in the world. The people who made them were semi-sedentary hunter-gatherers who built pit-house villages, conducted long-distance trade in obsidian and jade, and developed complex ritual practices centred on clay figurines called dogū.

Jōmon communities were remarkably adaptable, exploiting diverse environments from Hokkaidō to Kyushu. Marine resources were central to coastal groups, evidenced by enormous shell mounds (kaizuka). Population estimates for the Jōmon peak (c. 5,000 BCE) range up to 260,000 — significant for a pre-agricultural society.

Society and ritual

Jōmon society was organised around small, relatively egalitarian bands, though status differences appear in differential burial goods. Dogū figurines, often female in form, were frequently broken deliberately — suggesting ritual use. The Sannai-Maruyama site in Aomori (c. 5,900–4,200 BCE) revealed a large planned settlement with evidence of chestnut cultivation, pushing back evidence for intentional plant management.

dates: Wet-rice farming spreads from N. Kyushu
Queen Himiko sends envoy to Wei China
sections.body:
Around 300–400 BCE, wet-rice agriculture arrived in northern Kyushu, brought by migrants from the Korean peninsula. The incoming groups brought bronze mirrors, bells (dōtaku), and iron tools. The Yayoi period (c. 300 BCE – 300 CE) saw rapid population growth, permanent field systems, surplus production, and social stratification.

Chinese sources, particularly the Gishi Wajinden (Wei Zhi), provide the first written records of Japanese society. They describe a polity called Yamatai ruled by a shaman-queen named Himiko (c. 175–248 CE). Himiko never married; she communicated divine will while her brother handled political affairs. The location of Yamatai — in northern Kyushu or the Kinai region — remains one of Japanese archaeology's great unsolved debates.

The Jōmon-to-Yayoi transition models a recurring theme in Japanese history: the absorption of continental influences without wholesale replacement of existing culture. Jōmon spiritual traditions persisted into Shinto; Yayoi agricultural organisation provided the template for later state-building.

Exam angle: Be prepared to compare the Jōmon-Yayoi transition with later episodes of cultural borrowing (e.g., Tang-influenced Nara reforms). The pattern of selective, transformative adoption is a through-line in Japanese history.

terms: 'Cord-marked'; Japan's hunter-gatherer era; world's oldest pottery
Period of agricultural transition; named for Tokyo neighbourhood where pottery was found
Clay figurines of the Jōmon period; ritual function debated
Bronze bells of the Yayoi period; ritual use; found in western Japan
Powerful polity ruled by Queen Himiko; documented in Chinese chronicles
Shaman-queen of Yamatai; first named individual in Japanese history
Section of the Chinese Wei Zhi; first written account of Japan
Shell mounds; archaeological archives of coastal Jōmon communities

quiz.q: What is the primary characteristic that gives the Jōmon period its name?
opts: Rice cultivation
Cord-marked pottery
Bronze mirrors
Burial mounds
quiz.exp: Jōmon (縄文) means 'cord-marked' — referring to the distinctive patterns pressed into clay pottery, among the world's oldest fired ceramics.

quiz.q: Which Chinese text provides the earliest written description of Japanese society, including Queen Himiko?
opts: The Kojiki
The Nihon Shoki
The Wei Zhi (Gishi Wajinden)
The Taihō Code
quiz.exp: The Gishi Wajinden, part of the Wei Zhi (Chronicles of Wei, c. 297 CE), describes the polity of Yamatai and its ruler Himiko — the first written account of Japan.

quiz.q: The Yayoi culture primarily arrived in Japan from:
opts: Southern China by sea
The Korean peninsula
The Ryukyu islands
Northeastern Siberia
quiz.exp: Yayoi culture arrived principally from the Korean peninsula, bringing wet-rice agriculture, bronze, and iron — confirmed by archaeological distribution patterns and ancient DNA studies.

quiz.q: What does modern ancient-DNA research tell us about the relationship between Jōmon and Yayoi peoples?
opts: Jōmon people were entirely replaced
Yayoi people absorbed Jōmon without mixing
The two populations mixed genetically
Jōmon and Yayoi lived in complete separation
quiz.exp: Genetic studies confirm admixture between incoming Yayoi migrants and existing Jōmon populations — a blending that shaped the genetic profile of modern Japanese people.

quiz.q: Which of the following best describes Jōmon social organisation?
opts: Rigidly stratified kingdoms
Semi-sedentary hunter-gatherer bands with trade networks
Fully agricultural village communes
Nomadic pastoral clans
quiz.exp: Jōmon communities were semi-sedentary hunter-gatherers who built pit-house villages and conducted long-distance trade in obsidian and jade, with some evidence of incipient cultivation at later sites.

sources.text: Habu, Junko. Ancient Jōmon of Japan. Cambridge University Press, 2004.
Barnes, Gina L. State Formation in Japan: Emergence of a 4th-century Ruling Elite. Routledge, 2007.
Mizoguchi, Koji. The Archaeology of Japan: From the Earliest Rice Farming Villages to the Rise of the State. Cambridge University Press, 2013.
Kaner, Simon (ed.). The Power of Dogu: Ceramic Figures from Ancient Japan. British Museum Press, 2009.
Gishi Wajinden (Wei Zhi, section on Wa) — primary source, c. 297 CE. Trans. in Tsunoda, Ryusaku. Japan in the Chinese Dynastic Histories. Perkins Asiatic Monographs, 1951.

name: Kofun Era & Yamato State
intro: From the burial mounds of powerful chiefs to the adoption of Buddhism and Chinese writing, the Kofun era represents Japan's emergence as a recognisable state — one that consciously shaped itself by importing and transforming continental culture.

sections.body:
The Kofun period (c. 250–710 CE) takes its name from the large burial mounds (kofun) erected for powerful regional chiefs. The most iconic form is the zenpōkōenfun — a keyhole-shaped mound combining a square front with a circular rear. The Daisen Kofun in Sakai City, attributed to Emperor Nintoku, is one of the largest burial structures on earth by surface area.

Kofun were filled with grave goods signalling status: bronze mirrors, iron weapons and armour, jewellery of curved jade beads (magatama), and elaborate gilt-bronze horse trappings. Clay haniwa figurines were arranged around the mound's exterior. Over time, kofun construction spread from the Kinai region across most of Honshū, tracing the expansion of Yamato political influence.

dates: Japan sends students to Tang China
sections.body:
Buddhism arrived officially in 552 CE as a gift from the Baekje kingdom. Its reception ignited Japan's first documented religious-political conflict. The immigrant Soga clan clashed with the nativist Mononobe clan. The Soga victory (587 CE) determined that Buddhism would become the religion of state.

Prince Shōtoku (574–622), acting as regent for Empress Suiko, institutionalised Buddhism and created the framework for a centralised state. His 17-Article Constitution (604 CE) promoted Buddhist principles, Confucian hierarchy, and loyalty to the sovereign. Shōtoku also dispatched embassies to the Sui court on equal terms, famously addressing the Sui emperor as the Son of Heaven 'in the land where the sun rises' — a diplomatic assertion of parity that reportedly infuriated the Chinese court.

Taika Reform (645 CE): Following a coup eliminating the Soga clan, reformers proclaimed the Taika ('Great Change') Reform, announcing nationalisation of land and establishment of a Chinese-style administrative system. The reforms were only partially implemented, but they set the direction for the ritsuryō system.

terms: Burial mound; keyhole-shaped tombs of Yamato-era chiefs
Hollow clay figures placed around kofun
Curved comma-shaped jewels; one of Japan's three imperial regalia
Powerful immigrant clan who championed Buddhism against the Mononobe
Regent for Empress Suiko; Buddhism patron; 17-Article Constitution
Embassies sent to Tang China; conduit for institutional and cultural borrowing
Keyhole-shaped burial mound; signature form of Kofun-period elite tombs

quiz.q: The Daisen Kofun, one of the world's largest burial structures, is associated with which emperor?
opts: Emperor Jimmu
Emperor Nintoku
Emperor Shōmu
Emperor Kanmu
quiz.exp: The Daisen Kofun in Sakai City is attributed to Emperor Nintoku (early 5th century). It covers a surface area comparable to the Great Pyramid of Giza.

quiz.q: Which clan's defeat in 587 CE determined that Buddhism would be embraced by the Yamato state?
opts: The Fujiwara clan
The Minamoto clan
The Mononobe clan
The Taira clan
quiz.exp: The Mononobe clan, who opposed Buddhism in favour of native kami worship, were defeated by the Soga clan — securing Buddhism's place as Japan's state religion.

quiz.q: Prince Shōtoku's 17-Article Constitution (604 CE) was primarily:
opts: A criminal law code
A moral guide for officials promoting Buddhist and Confucian values
A military code for samurai
A trade agreement with China
quiz.exp: The 17-Article Constitution was a moral and philosophical document, not a legal code. It emphasised harmony, Buddhist ideals, and loyalty to the sovereign, drawing on both Buddhist and Confucian thought.

quiz.q: The Taika Reform of 645 CE was significant because it:
opts: Ended Buddhism in Japan
Introduced rice cultivation
Attempted to nationalise land and create a Chinese-style bureaucracy
Established the first shogunate
quiz.exp: The Taika Reform proclaimed nationalisation of all land and establishment of a centralised bureaucratic state on the Tang model. Implementation was uneven but it set the direction for the ritsuryō system.

quiz.q: Japan's diplomatic correspondence with the Sui dynasty was remarkable for:
opts: Acknowledging China's cultural superiority
Requesting military aid
Addressing the Chinese emperor as an equal rather than a superior
Refusing all contact with China
quiz.exp: Shōtoku's famous letter began 'From the Son of Heaven in the land where the sun rises to the Son of Heaven in the land where the sun sets' — a claim of diplomatic equality that reportedly angered the Sui court.

name: Nara Period
intro: Japan's first permanent capital gave the Nara period its name, but the era's true significance lies in what was built around it: a Chinese-style legal state, a national Buddhist infrastructure, and the foundational texts of Japanese literary and historical tradition.

dates: Permanent private ownership of reclaimed land permitted
sections.body:
The Nara period (710–794) represents the fullest expression of the ritsuryō state — a legal and administrative system modelled directly on Tang China. The Taihō Code of 701 CE divided law into ritsu (criminal law) and ryō (administrative law). It established a central bureaucracy headed by the Grand Council of State (Dajō-kan), divided the country into provinces and districts, and created an elaborate court-rank system.

The handen shūju-hō (land allotment system) assigned rice paddies to commoners every six years based on census records. The system proved difficult to maintain: population growth, natural disasters, and evasion of census registration steadily eroded the state's tax base. The Three-Generation Law of 723 (extended to permanent ownership in 743) allowed private retention of reclaimed land — the first crack in the nationalised land ideal, eventually leading to the shōen (private estates) that would define the medieval period.

dates: Shōmu orders kokubunji in all provinces
sections.body:
Emperor Shōmu (r. 724–749) elevated state Buddhism to its apogee. Faced with a devastating smallpox epidemic, crop failures, and political instability, Shōmu turned to Buddhism for state protection. In 741 CE he ordered kokubunji (provincial temples) built in every province. The centrepiece was the Tōdai-ji Great Buddha — a colossal bronze image of Rushana (Vairocana), approximately 15 metres tall, dedicated in 752.

The monk Dōkyō rose to extraordinary influence under Empress Shōtoku (r. 764–770), receiving the title Hōō (Dharma King) and reportedly coming close to being named emperor. The Usa Hachiman oracle declared no one outside the imperial line should ascend the throne. Dōkyō was exiled after Shōtoku's death — and no woman ruled as empress regnant again for over a millennium.

The Kojiki (712, 'Record of Ancient Matters') records the age of the gods through the reign of Empress Suiko, written partly in man'yōgana (Chinese characters used phonetically). The Nihon Shoki (720) covers similar ground in formal classical Chinese — Japan's face to the continent. The Man'yōshū (c. 759, 'Collection of Ten Thousand Leaves') contains over 4,500 poems by more than 450 poets — emperors, aristocrats, frontier soldiers, and anonymous farmers.

Why Nara ended: Three converging crises forced the move: (1) political danger of powerful Buddhist institutions after the Dōkyō affair; (2) fiscal collapse of the handen land system; (3) Emperor Kanmu's determination to break from an exhausted political order. The court moved to Nagaoka-kyō (784), then Heian-kyō (Kyoto) in 794.

terms: Legal-administrative system modelled on Tang China; criminal + administrative codes
Land allotment system; rice paddies assigned every 6 years by census
Provincial temples ordered by Shōmu in every province (741)
Head temple in Nara housing the Great Buddha (Rushana Daibutsu)
712; Japan's oldest chronicle; mythology and imperial legitimation
720; Japan's second chronicle; formal Chinese; diplomatic history
c.759; oldest poetry anthology; 4,500+ poems; wide social range
Monk who rose to political power under Empress Shōtoku; exiled after her death
Phonetic use of Chinese characters to write Japanese; precursor to kana

quiz.q: The Taihō Code (701) divided law into ritsu and ryō, meaning:
opts: Imperial law and provincial law
Criminal law and administrative law
Buddhist law and Shinto law
Military law and civil law
quiz.exp: Ritsu (律) covered criminal law; ryō (令) covered administrative law. Together they formed the ritsuryō system — Japan's first comprehensive legal code based on Tang Chinese models.

quiz.q: Emperor Shōmu's construction of the Tōdai-ji Great Buddha was motivated primarily by:
opts: Desire to impress Chinese envoys
National protection during epidemic and political crises
A personal vow after military victory
Pressure from Buddhist monks at court
quiz.exp: Shōmu commissioned the Rushana Daibutsu against a backdrop of devastating smallpox epidemics (735–37), crop failures, and political instability — framing it as an act of state protection through Buddhist merit.

quiz.q: What distinguishes the Kojiki (712) from the Nihon Shoki (720)?
opts: The Kojiki was written in kana; Nihon Shoki in Chinese
The Kojiki covers earlier mythology only
The Kojiki used man'yōgana for Japanese sounds; Nihon Shoki was in formal Chinese for continental audiences
The Kojiki was destroyed; only Nihon Shoki survives
quiz.exp: The Kojiki (712) used a mixed script including man'yōgana for domestic audiences, focusing on mythological legitimation. The Nihon Shoki (720) was written in formal classical Chinese, intended as Japan's official history for continental audiences.

quiz.q: The Dōkyō affair (760s–770s) had which lasting consequence?
opts: Buddhism was banned from the imperial court
No woman ruled as empress regnant again for over a millennium
The capital was moved to Osaka
The ritsuryō system was abolished
quiz.exp: The near-usurpation of the throne by the monk Dōkyō under Empress Shōtoku alarmed the court so severely that no empress regnant would rule again until the modern era.

quiz.q: The handen shūju-hō land allotment system broke down primarily because:
opts: Foreign invasion destroyed census records
Population growth, census evasion, and new laws allowing private land ownership eroded the tax base
Emperor Kanmu abolished it when he moved to Kyoto
Buddhist temples seized all agricultural land
quiz.exp: The handen system required regular census records and consistent rice yields. Population growth, peasant evasion, and the 743 law permitting permanent ownership of reclaimed land all contributed to its collapse — laying groundwork for the shōen estate system.

name: Heian Period
intro: The longest imperial era in Japanese history was also its most culturally brilliant — and its most politically paradoxical. While aristocrats in Kyoto refined poetry and literature to extraordinary levels, power quietly bled away toward provincial warriors who would soon remake Japan entirely.

sections.h2: Fujiwara Dominance and the Insei System
sections.body:
Emperor Kanmu moved the capital to Heian-kyō (present-day Kyoto) in 794, partly to escape the entangled influence of Nara's Buddhist temples. The dominant political story of the Heian period is the rise of the Fujiwara clan through an elegant mechanism: marrying their daughters into the imperial family and serving as sesshō (regent for a child emperor) or kampaku (regent for an adult emperor). Fujiwara no Michinaga (966–1027) represented the peak — three of his daughters became empress consorts.

By the late 11th century, emperors fought back through the insei system: retiring from the throne (escaping Fujiwara regency) while continuing to exercise real power as Retired Emperor (In). Emperor Shirakawa (retired 1086) pioneered this approach, governing for decades after abdication.

dates: Sei Shōnagon writes The Pillow Book
sections.body:
The Heian court produced one of the world's great literary efflorescences, driven by aristocratic women. The development of kana (hiragana and katakana) gave educated women a distinctly Japanese script. Men wrote official documents in Chinese; women wrote in Japanese — producing a body of vernacular literature of extraordinary sophistication.

Lady Murasaki Shikibu (c. 973–1014) wrote the Genji Monogatari (The Tale of Genji, c. 1008) — 54 chapters following the romantic and political life of the fictional 'shining prince' Hikaru Genji. Widely regarded as the world's first psychological novel, it is notable for mono no aware (the pathos of transient things) and complex female interiority. Sei Shōnagon's Makura no Sōshi (The Pillow Book) captures Heian aesthetic sensibility with sparkling wit.

sections.h2: The Rise of the Warriors and the Genpei War
dates: Hōgen Disturbance; samurai enter capital politics
Taira no Kiyomori takes control of government
Battle of Dan-no-ura ends Heian period
sections.body:
The collapse of the ritsuryō land system and the growth of shōen (private tax-exempt estates) created provincial warrior clans. Two clans — the Taira and the Minamoto — rose to national prominence. Taira no Kiyomori effectively took over the government by 1179 — the first warrior to do so. The Genpei War (1180–85) ended at the naval Battle of Dan-no-ura (1185), where the Taira were annihilated and child emperor Antoku drowned.

The shōen connection: As private estates multiplied and escaped central taxation, the government's revenue and administrative reach shrank. Provincial warriors who provided security became estate managers and accumulated local power — the structural cause of samurai dominance.

terms: Regent for a child emperor; Fujiwara mechanism of control
Regent for an adult emperor; the other Fujiwara regency title
Rule by a retired emperor; mechanism to escape Fujiwara control
Private tax-exempt estates; undermined the ritsuryō fiscal system
'Pathos of things'; central Heian aesthetic of transient beauty
The Tale of Genji; c.1008; world's first psychological novel
1180–85 civil war between Minamoto and Taira; ended Heian period
Phonetic Japanese scripts (hiragana/katakana); enabled women's literature
905 CE poetry anthology; contrast with Man'yōshū for exam purposes

quiz.q: The Fujiwara clan maintained political dominance primarily through:
opts: Control of the military
Marrying daughters into the imperial family and serving as regents
Monopoly of Buddhist institutions
Direct ownership of all provincial land
quiz.exp: The Fujiwara placed their daughters as imperial consorts and served as sesshō (regent for child emperors) or kampaku (regent for adult emperors) — governing without holding imperial office.

quiz.q: The Tale of Genji (c.1008) was written by a woman partly because:
opts: Men were prohibited from writing fiction
Kana scripts were associated with women's writing while men used Chinese for official purposes
The author disguised her identity
Women had more leisure time than men at court
quiz.exp: Kana (hiragana) was associated with vernacular Japanese writing used by women, while educated men wrote official documents in Chinese. This gave aristocratic women the medium for Heian's greatest literature.

quiz.q: The insei system (rule by retired emperors) was developed primarily to:
opts: Give emperors more time for religious practice
Escape Fujiwara regency control while retaining real power
Allow older men to enjoy retirement
Consolidate Buddhist and imperial authority
quiz.exp: By retiring from the throne (releasing them from Fujiwara kampaku regency) while continuing to govern as Retired Emperor, figures like Shirakawa reclaimed actual political power from the Fujiwara.

quiz.q: The growth of shōen estates contributed to samurai power because:
opts: Shōen owners hired samurai who accumulated regional influence
Samurai received shōen as rewards from the emperor
Shōen estates were required to train samurai
The ritsuryō system created shōen specifically for warrior clans
quiz.exp: As private estates multiplied and escaped central taxation, the government's revenue shrank. Provincial warriors who provided security became estate managers and accumulated land, followers, and local power.

quiz.q: The Genpei War (1180–85) ended with:
opts: A negotiated peace
The Taira clan's destruction at the naval Battle of Dan-no-ura
The restoration of Fujiwara regency
The abdication of the Minamoto leader
quiz.exp: The Battle of Dan-no-ura (1185) was a decisive Minamoto naval victory. The Taira were annihilated; child emperor Antoku drowned. Minamoto Yoritomo then established Japan's first military government at Kamakura.

name: Kamakura Shogunate
intro: Japan's first military government was also its first experiment with dual sovereignty — maintaining an imperial court in Kyoto while real power resided with the shogun's administration in Kamakura. This institutional arrangement, and the crises it survived, defined samurai governance for centuries.

dates: Yoritomo controls Japan after Genpei War
sections.body:
Minamoto no Yoritomo established his base at Kamakura — geographically defensible and distant from Kyoto's entanglements. In 1192, he received the title Seii Taishogun from the emperor, giving his military government (bakufu) formal legitimacy. The result was Japan's first explicit dual polity: the imperial court retained cultural prestige and nominal sovereignty; the bakufu controlled military affairs through a network of shugo (military governors) and jitō (estate stewards).

Yoritomo died in 1199. Power passed to the Hōjō clan, who served as shikken (regent) to the shogun — creating a three-level structure: emperor → shogun → Hōjō regent. The Hōjō cemented authority by defeating Retired Emperor Go-Toba's coup in the Jōkyū War of 1221.

sections.h2: The Mongol Invasions and New Buddhism
sections.body:
Kublai Khan demanded Japanese submission in 1268. The Hōjō regent refused. The first invasion (1274) brought 25,000–33,000 troops — Japanese defenders were shocked by explosive projectiles and massed arrow fire. The second invasion (1281) involved perhaps 140,000 troops; after weeks of fighting, a powerful typhoon (kamikaze, 'divine wind') destroyed much of the Mongol fleet. The invasions were repelled but created a fiscal crisis: warriors who fought expected land rewards, but no enemy land was captured.

The Kamakura period saw the emergence of distinctly Japanese Buddhist schools: Pure Land (Jōdo-shū) offered salvation through the nembutsu prayer — accessible to all. Nichiren Buddhism insisted exclusively on the Lotus Sutra. Zen (Rinzai and Sōtō) emphasised meditation and direct experience, appealing especially to warriors.

terms: Military governors appointed by the bakufu to provinces
Estate stewards who managed land and collected taxes for the bakufu
Hōjō regent — controlled the shogun; third layer of Kamakura government
1221; Hōjō victory over Retired Emperor Go-Toba; cemented bakufu dominance
'Divine wind'; typhoons that destroyed Mongol invasion fleets (1274, 1281)
'Namu Amida Butsu'; Pure Land Buddhist practice; accessible to all
Emperor retains ritual sovereignty; shogun holds military-administrative power

quiz.q: The Kamakura bakufu is best described as a:
opts: Replacement of the imperial system
Dual polity where the court retained ritual authority and the shogunate held military-administrative power
Democratic government elected by warriors
Theocratic state combining Buddhist and imperial authority
quiz.exp: The Kamakura system was explicitly dual: the emperor in Kyoto retained ceremonial sovereignty; the Kamakura shogunate controlled military affairs and land dispute adjudication through shugo and jitō.

quiz.q: After Yoritomo's death, real power in Kamakura passed to the Hōjō clan acting as:
opts: Shogun
Retired Shogun
Shikken (regent to the shogun)
Kampaku
quiz.exp: The Hōjō served as shikken (regent) to the shogun — creating a three-tier structure: emperor → shogun → Hōjō regent. This layered indirect rule became a recurring feature of Japanese governance.

quiz.q: The Jōkyū War (1221) demonstrated that:
opts: The emperor could reassert power over the bakufu
The Hōjō could militarily and politically dominate the imperial court
The Minamoto clan survived Yoritomo's death
Buddhism could mediate between court and warriors
quiz.exp: Retired Emperor Go-Toba's attempted coup failed completely. The Hōjō confiscated his estates, exiled him, and installed a new emperor — proving the bakufu could override imperial authority.

quiz.q: The Mongol invasions created a fiscal crisis for the Kamakura bakufu because:
opts: The invasions destroyed Japan's rice crop
Warriors expected land rewards for fighting but no enemy land was available to redistribute
The invasions were lost and Japan paid tribute
Kublai Khan imposed trade embargoes
quiz.exp: Japanese warfare traditionally rewarded warriors with captured land. Since the Mongols were repelled rather than conquered, no new land was available to distribute. Warriors went unrewarded, undermining the bakufu's authority.

quiz.q: Which Kamakura-era Buddhist movement is most associated with accessibility to ordinary people through a simple prayer practice?
opts: Zen (Rinzai)
Kegon
Pure Land (Jōdo-shū)
Shingon
quiz.exp: Pure Land Buddhism, founded by Hōnen, taught salvation through repetition of the nembutsu ('Namu Amida Butsu') — a practice accessible to illiterate farmers and women, not just learned monks or elite warriors.

name: Muromachi & Sengoku Periods
intro: The Muromachi shogunate presided over one of Japan's great cultural flowerings — Noh theatre, the tea ceremony, ink painting — before its authority collapsed into a century of civil war that transformed the political landscape and set the stage for reunification.

sections.h2: The Ashikaga Shogunate and Muromachi Culture
dates: Ashikaga Takauji establishes shogunate in Kyoto
Tally trade with Ming China begins
sections.body:
Ashikaga Takauji established his shogunate in the Muromachi district of Kyoto — at the cultural centre rather than separate from it. The third shogun, Yoshimitsu (r. 1368–1394), patronised Noh theatre (created by Zeami Motokiyo), resumed diplomatic trade with Ming China under the tally trade system, and built the Golden Pavilion (Kinkaku-ji). Later shoguns patronised renga (linked verse), ink-wash painting, and the formalised chanoyu (tea ceremony).

The shogunate's legitimacy was initially contested by the Nanbokuchō (Northern and Southern Courts) split (1336–1392) — Go-Daigo's rival Southern Court generated significant debate about legitimate succession.

sections.h2: The Ōnin War and the Sengoku Period
dates: Ōnin War ends; Sengoku period begins
Francis Xavier arrives; Jesuit missions begin
sections.body:
The Ōnin War (1467–77) began as a dispute over shogunal succession and reduced much of Kyoto to ashes. The shogunate never recovered its authority. The Sengoku ('Warring States') period (c. 1467–1573) followed — roughly a century of near-constant warfare in which daimyō competed for territory. The concept of gekokujō ('the low overturning the high') captures the era's social fluidity.

The arrival of Portuguese traders at Tanegashima in 1543 introduced firearms that would transform Japanese warfare. The Jesuit missionary Francis Xavier arrived in 1549, beginning a Christian mission that would at its peak count several hundred thousand converts.

Why Sengoku matters for the exam: The Sengoku period's social upheaval explains why the Three Unifiers could emerge from relatively humble backgrounds, and why their social-control measures (Sword Hunt, land surveys) were so significant — they were systematically reversing the gekokujō dynamic.

terms: Northern and Southern Court split (1336–1392); rival imperial lines
Regional warlords of the Sengoku period; controlled autonomous domains
1467–77; decade of war in Kyoto; triggered the Sengoku period
'Warring States' period, c.1467–1573; near-constant civil war
'The low overturning the high'; social inversion characteristic of Sengoku
Classical theatre patronised by Yoshimitsu; created by Zeami Motokiyo
Tea ceremony; developed in Muromachi; formalised by Sen no Rikyū
Tally trade system with Ming China; resumed by Ashikaga Yoshimitsu

quiz.q: The Ōnin War (1467–77) is historically significant primarily because:
opts: It ended the imperial line's authority permanently
It destroyed Ashikaga authority and triggered the Sengoku century of civil war
It enabled Japan's unification under the Ashikaga
It introduced firearms to Japanese warfare
quiz.exp: The Ōnin War devastated Kyoto and shattered the shogunate's authority. It triggered the Sengoku ('Warring States') period — roughly a century of unconstrained regional warfare.

quiz.q: Gekokujō, a concept associated with the Sengoku period, means:
opts: The divine right of the emperor
Loyalty unto death
The low overturning the high — subordinates displacing lords
The way of the warrior
quiz.exp: Gekokujō (下剋上) describes the social inversion characteristic of the Sengoku period, when subordinates regularly overthrew and killed their lords and men of humble origin built large domains.

quiz.q: Which Ashikaga shogun patronised Noh theatre and resumed trade with Ming China?
opts: Ashikaga Takauji
Ashikaga Yoshimitsu
Ashikaga Yoshimasa
Ashikaga Yoshiaki
quiz.exp: Ashikaga Yoshimitsu (r. 1368–1394), the third shogun, was the cultural and political peak of the Muromachi period. He patronised Zeami's Noh theatre, built Kinkaku-ji, and resumed diplomatic trade with Ming China.

quiz.q: Portuguese firearms arrived in Japan in 1543 and within decades had:
opts: Been banned by the shogunate
Transformed battlefield tactics; massed arquebusier formations replaced cavalry charges
Been adopted only by Christian daimyō
Remained rare due to manufacturing difficulties
quiz.exp: Japanese craftsmen quickly reverse-engineered Portuguese arquebuses. By the 1570s, Oda Nobunaga was using massed firearms formations (most famously at Nagashino, 1575) that made traditional samurai cavalry tactics obsolete.

quiz.q: The Ashikaga shogunate was located in Kyoto rather than Kamakura primarily because:
opts: Kamakura was destroyed in the Genpei War
The Ashikaga wanted proximity to the imperial court and its cultural prestige
Kyoto had better defensive geography
Zen temples in Kyoto required shogunal supervision
quiz.exp: Ashikaga Takauji deliberately placed his bakufu in Kyoto's Muromachi district to be at the political and cultural centre — enabling the cultural synthesis between aristocratic and warrior aesthetics that defined Muromachi culture.

name: Azuchi-Momoyama Period
intro: Three extraordinary individuals ended a century of civil war and forged the political and social framework that would govern Japan for the next two and a half centuries. Their methods differed sharply; their combined achievement was the reunification of the archipelago.

dates: Battle of Okehazama; Nobunaga defeats Imagawa
Nobunaga burns Enryaku-ji on Mt. Hiei
Battle of Nagashino; massed firearms deployed
sections.body: Oda Nobunaga (1534–1582) came from a minor daimyō family in Owari province. Over two decades he subdued rivals across central Japan, deposed the last Ashikaga shogun in 1573, and controlled nearly a third of the country before his death. He deployed firearms in disciplined massed formations — most spectacularly at Nagashino (1575), where rows of arquebusiers firing in rotation destroyed the Takeda cavalry. He promoted rakuichi rakuza (free markets) and violently destroyed Buddhist military power, most notoriously burning the Enryaku-ji complex on Mt. Hiei in 1571. He was assassinated at Honnō-ji in 1582 by his general Akechi Mitsuhide.

Toyotomi Hideyoshi (1537–1598), of peasant origin, completed unification by 1590. His Taikō-kenchi (land survey) systematically measured rice yields across Japan. The Sword Hunt of 1588 confiscated weapons from farmers and townspeople, crystallising the distinction between the warrior class and the agricultural population. His Korean invasions (1592, 1597) failed militarily and exhausted resources. When Hideyoshi died in 1598, he left a five-year-old heir.

Tokugawa Ieyasu, the most powerful regent, won the decisive Battle of Sekigahara (1600) and received the title of shogun in 1603.

The Three Unifiers compared (classic exam question): Nobunaga pounded the rice cake — destroyed the old order. Hideyoshi kneaded it — built the social structure. Ieyasu sat down and ate it — institutionalised it into a system lasting 260+ years. Each built on his predecessor's foundation.

terms: Free markets, abolition of guild monopolies; Nobunaga's commercial policy
Hideyoshi's systematic national land survey; fixed tax rates
1588; Hideyoshi's confiscation of weapons from non-samurai
1575; Nobunaga's massed arquebusier tactics destroyed Takeda cavalry
1582; Nobunaga's assassination by his general Akechi Mitsuhide
1600; Ieyasu's decisive victory leading to the Tokugawa shogunate
1592 and 1597 Korean invasion campaigns ordered by Hideyoshi
Nobunaga (destroyed old order), Hideyoshi (built framework), Ieyasu (institutionalised)

quiz.q: Oda Nobunaga's treatment of Buddhist establishments (including burning Enryaku-ji) was motivated primarily by:
opts: Personal conversion to Christianity
Desire to appropriate Buddhist wealth
Eliminating the political and military power of institutions that opposed him
Shinto nativist ideology
quiz.exp: Nobunaga attacked Buddhist establishments because they actively opposed his unification with military force. This was primarily a political-military decision, not an anti-religious one.

quiz.q: Hideyoshi's Sword Hunt of 1588 is significant because it:
opts: Disarmed all samurai
Crystallised the distinction between the warrior class and commoners, fixing social boundaries
Collected weapons for the Korean invasion
Was immediately reversed by Tokugawa Ieyasu
quiz.exp: By confiscating weapons from farmers, priests, and townspeople, the Sword Hunt institutionalised the boundary between bushi (warriors) and the rest of the population — foundational to the rigid Tokugawa social order.

quiz.q: The Battle of Sekigahara (1600) was fought between:
opts: The Toyotomi and the Ming Chinese
Ieyasu's eastern coalition and a western coalition loyal to the Toyotomi heir
Hideyoshi and Nobunaga's remnant forces
The Shimazu and Mōri clans
quiz.exp: Sekigahara was the decisive confrontation between Tokugawa Ieyasu's eastern forces and a western coalition nominally defending Toyotomi Hideyori. Ieyasu's victory opened the path to the shogunate.

quiz.q: Hideyoshi's Korean invasions (1592, 1597) ended in:
opts: Japanese conquest of Korea
Military failure and exhaustion of Japanese resources
Korean acceptance of Japanese suzerainty
A negotiated partition
quiz.exp: Both invasions ultimately failed. Korean resistance (including Admiral Yi Sun-sin's naval genius), Ming Chinese intervention, and overextended supply lines led to withdrawal. The campaigns exhausted Japan.

quiz.q: The saying 'Nobunaga pounded the rice cake, Hideyoshi kneaded it, Ieyasu ate it' primarily conveys:
opts: Their different social origins
Their sequential contributions and contrasting methods
The different regions they controlled
Their religious affiliations
quiz.exp: The saying captures their complementary roles: Nobunaga destroyed the old order; Hideyoshi built the social and administrative framework; Ieyasu institutionalised it into a durable system lasting 260+ years.

name: The Edo Period
intro: The Tokugawa peace lasted over two and a half centuries — an extraordinary achievement of social engineering and institutional design. Beneath its rigid surface, however, new social forces were accumulating that would overwhelm the system when the outside world forced its way back in.

sections.body:
The roughly 270 daimyō were divided into fudai (hereditary Tokugawa vassals) in strategically sensitive domains and tozama (outside lords, former enemies at Sekigahara) in distant domains and excluded from key offices. The most elegant control mechanism was sankin-kōtai (alternate attendance): daimyō spent alternate years in Edo and their home domains, leaving families in Edo as permanent hostages. The system imposed enormous expense, keeping daimyō financially weakened.

Tokugawa society was officially stratified into four ranks: samurai (shi), farmers (nō), artisans (kō), and merchants (shō) — the shi-nō-kō-shō order — with outcaste groups below. In practice, wealthy merchants often held more real economic power than impoverished samurai.

dates: Dutch confined to Dejima; sakoku complete
Perry's Black Ships arrive at Uraga
sections.body:
The sakoku policy expelled virtually all foreigners and banned overseas travel. Dutch traders were confined to Dejima in Nagasaki. From 1720, relaxation of book import rules enabled rangaku (Dutch learning) — study of Western science, medicine, and geography through Dutch intermediaries.

Far from stagnation, the Edo period was one of Japan's most culturally productive eras. Urban merchant culture (chōnin) produced kabuki theatre, ukiyo-e woodblock prints (Hokusai, Hiroshige), and haiku reaching its height with Matsuo Bashō. Japan's literacy rates reached levels comparable to Western Europe.

US Commodore Matthew Perry's arrival in 1853 forced the bakufu to open ports. The Ansei Treaties of 1858 granted extraterritoriality and fixed tariffs — humiliating concessions. The sonnō jōi ('revere the emperor, expel the barbarians') movement grew. After the Boshin War (1868–69), the Tokugawa shogunate fell.

Sankin-kōtai's unexpected legacy: By requiring daimyō processions to Edo and back, the system made Japan's highway network among the world's most heavily trafficked — stimulating commerce, communications, and a shared national culture that made rapid modernisation post-1868 easier.

terms: Alternate attendance; daimyō spent alternating years in Edo; families as hostages
Hereditary Tokugawa vassals; placed in strategic domains
Outside lords; former enemies at Sekigahara; excluded from key offices
'Closed country'; isolation policy; Dutch and Chinese only at Nagasaki
Artificial island in Nagasaki; sole Dutch trading post during sakoku
'Dutch learning'; Western science filtered through Nagasaki
Urban merchant/artisan class; patrons of Edo popular culture
Woodblock print tradition; Hokusai, Hiroshige; the 'floating world'

quiz.q: The sankin-kōtai system controlled daimyō primarily through:
opts: Annual military inspections
Requiring alternate residence in Edo with families left as hostages, imposing crippling expenses
Confiscating domain revenues annually
Requiring daimyō to marry Tokugawa women
quiz.exp: Sankin-kōtai required daimyō to alternate between Edo and their domains, maintaining expensive Edo residences. Their families remained in Edo as de facto hostages, making rebellion logistically and politically very difficult.

quiz.q: During the sakoku period, which European nation maintained the sole Western trading contact with Japan?
opts: Portugal
Spain
England
The Netherlands (Dutch)
quiz.exp: The Dutch East India Company (VOC) was confined to Dejima in Nagasaki — the only Western trading contact permitted during sakoku. Portugal was expelled after the Shimabara Rebellion.

quiz.q: The Confucian rationale for placing merchants below farmers in the four-tier hierarchy was:
opts: Merchants were foreign in origin
Merchants were associated with Buddhism
Merchants did not produce goods but merely traded, making them less socially valuable
Merchants were too wealthy to be trusted
quiz.exp: Neo-Confucian ideology valued those who produced (farmers grow food; artisans make goods) over those who merely facilitated exchange without creating value. In practice, wealthy merchants often held more economic power than impoverished samurai.

quiz.q: The 'Black Ships' incident (1853) was significant because:
opts: It led to Japan immediately declaring war on the US
It demonstrated the bakufu's inability to exclude foreign powers, triggering the political crisis leading to the Meiji Restoration
It resulted in an immediate opening of all Japanese ports
It caused the emperor to side with the Tokugawa against foreign threats
quiz.exp: Perry's visit revealed the bakufu's military weakness. The humiliating Ansei Treaties (1858) further delegitimised Tokugawa rule, strengthening the sonnō jōi movement and accelerating the crisis producing the Meiji Restoration.

quiz.q: Rangaku (Dutch learning) was significant because it:
opts: Converted large numbers of Japanese to Christianity
Created a body of intellectuals familiar with Western science, medicine, and military technology
Replaced Confucianism as Japan's official ideology
Led directly to the end of sakoku
quiz.exp: Through the Dutch connection at Nagasaki, a small but important group of Japanese scholars studied Western anatomy, astronomy, geography, and military technology — a knowledge base that accelerated modernisation after 1868.

jp: 明治・大正・昭和前期
name: Meiji Era Through WWII
intro: In less than eighty years, Japan transformed from a feudal shogunate into a modern industrial nation, achieved great-power status, built an overseas empire, and then gambled it all in a catastrophic war that ended with nuclear destruction and unconditional surrender.

dates: Satsuma Rebellion crushed by conscript army
sections.body:
The Meiji Restoration combined a genuine revolution in governance with a rhetorical restoration of imperial authority. The Charter Oath (1868) promised deliberative assemblies and knowledge sought worldwide. The abolition of domains and samurai stipends (1871–73) dismantled the feudal order.

The Iwakura Mission (1871–73) sent nearly half the Meiji government on an eighteen-month tour of the US and Europe. They returned convinced Japan must modernise comprehensively, and the state adopted a French-influenced civil code, German-influenced military, and American-influenced school system. The Satsuma Rebellion (1877), led by Saigō Takamori, was the last armed challenge by the old warrior class — crushed by the new conscript army. Itō Hirobumi drafted the Meiji Constitution of 1889: sovereignty in the emperor, military direct access to the throne bypassing the cabinet — a structural flaw that facilitated 1930s militarism.

sections.h2: Imperial Expansion, Taishō Democracy, and War
sections.body:
The Russo-Japanese War (1904–05) made Japan the first Asian nation in modern history to defeat a European great power. Korea was annexed in 1910. The Taishō period (1912–26) brought brief party government and universal male suffrage (1925). The Great Kantō Earthquake (1923) killed approximately 105,000 — followed by violence against Korean residents.

The Manchurian Incident (1931) established the pattern of military insubordination: Kwantung Army officers seized Manchuria without government authorisation and the government endorsed rather than punished them. Pearl Harbor (December 7, 1941) opened the Pacific War. The Battle of Midway (June 1942) destroyed four Japanese fleet carriers and ended Japan's strategic offensive capacity. Atomic bombs were dropped on Hiroshima (August 6) and Nagasaki (August 9, 1945). Hirohito announced surrender on August 15; formal instruments were signed September 2, 1945.

terms: 1868; five principles of Meiji governance; symbolic opening of new era
1871–73 government delegation to study Western institutions
Elder statesmen who wielded real power behind constitutional forms
1889; emperor sovereign; military direct access to throne; bicameral diet
1877; last samurai uprising; crushed by conscript army
1931; Kwantung Army seizes Manchuria without government orders
June 1942; loss of four carriers; turning point of Pacific War
Brief period of party government and civil liberties (1912–26); undermined by Depression

quiz.q: The Iwakura Mission (1871–73) was significant because:
opts: It negotiated the end of unequal treaties
It sent Japanese officials to study Western institutions, informing comprehensive modernisation policies
It established Japanese colonies in the Pacific
It negotiated the Anglo-Japanese Alliance
quiz.exp: The Iwakura Mission sent senior government officials on an 18-month tour of the West. They returned with detailed knowledge of Western legal, military, educational, and industrial institutions that directly shaped Meiji reforms.

quiz.q: The Meiji Constitution (1889) was most problematic in the long term because it:
opts: Abolished the emperor
Gave the military direct access to the throne, bypassing civilian cabinet control
Established universal suffrage
Banned political parties
quiz.exp: By granting the military direct access to the emperor (independent supreme command), the Meiji Constitution created a structural weakness that allowed military factions to bypass civilian government — facilitating militarism in the 1930s.

quiz.q: The Russo-Japanese War (1904–05) was historically significant globally because:
opts: Russia gained control of Korea
Japan demonstrated that an Asian nation could defeat a European great power in modern warfare
The United States mediated in Japan's favour
It led to the formation of the Axis powers
quiz.exp: Japan's victory shocked the world and reverberated across Asia, inspiring independence movements and challenging the assumption of European military supremacy. It established Japan as a great power in East Asia.

quiz.q: The Manchurian Incident (1931) revealed which structural problem?
opts: Civilian governments could control the military through the Diet
Military units could act independently and force the government to accept faits accomplis
The emperor directly commanded all military operations
Political parties had too much power over military appointments
quiz.exp: The Kwantung Army acted without government authorisation, seizing Manchuria and presenting Tokyo with a fait accompli. Rather than punishing the officers, the government endorsed the action — demonstrating civilian government's inability to control military factions.

quiz.q: The atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki occurred in which sequence?
opts: Both on the same day
Hiroshima August 6, Nagasaki August 9, 1945
Nagasaki first, then Hiroshima
One in July, one in August 1945
quiz.exp: The atomic bomb was dropped on Hiroshima on August 6, 1945, and on Nagasaki on August 9. The Soviet Union declared war on Japan on August 8 — three events in four days that prompted Hirohito's announcement of surrender on August 15.

name: Postwar Japan to the Present
intro: Defeat in 1945 brought American occupation, a new constitution, and sweeping social reforms. What followed was an economic miracle, a long stagnation, a series of natural disasters, and an ongoing reckoning with Japan's place in Asia — questions that remain unresolved in the Reiwa era.

sections.h2: Allied Occupation and the New Japan
dates: San Francisco Peace Treaty; US-Japan Security Treaty
sections.body:
The Allied Occupation (1945–52), effectively American under General MacArthur, implemented sweeping reforms. The new Constitution of 1947 contained Article 9, by which Japan renounced war and the maintenance of war potential. Women received the right to vote; the emperor became 'the symbol of the State and of the unity of the people, deriving his position from the will of the people.'

Land reform (1946–50) redistributed agricultural land from absentee landlords to tenant farmers. Zaibatsu (industrial conglomerates) were dissolved, though successor companies (keiretsu) quickly re-formed as looser networks. As the Cold War intensified, American policy 'reversed course' — emphasising Japanese economic recovery over democratisation. The 1951 San Francisco Peace Treaty restored sovereignty; simultaneously, the US-Japan Security Treaty allowed American military bases to remain, providing Japan's security while enabling minimal defence spending.

sections.h2: The Economic Miracle, Bubble, and Contemporary Japan
dates: Emperor Akihito abdicates; Reiwa era begins
sections.body:
Japan's postwar economic growth averaged approximately 10% annually through the 1960s. Japan became the world's second-largest economy by 1968. The 1964 Tokyo Olympics symbolised Japan's reintegration into the international community.

The Plaza Accord (1985) sharply appreciated the yen. Low interest rates and financial deregulation fuelled a massive asset bubble. The bubble collapsed in 1990–91, leading to the 'Lost Decade' of deflation, stagnant growth, and bank failures. The 3/11 disaster (March 11, 2011) combined a magnitude-9.0 earthquake, devastating tsunami (~19,000 deaths), and meltdowns at Fukushima Daiichi — Japan's worst peacetime crisis since 1945. Abe Shinzō's return to power (2012) brought 'Abenomics' — aggressive monetary easing, fiscal stimulus, and structural reforms — along with a controversial reinterpretation of Article 9 to permit 'collective self-defence.'

The Article 9 debate: As written, Article 9 prohibits maintaining war potential. Japan's Self-Defence Forces are justified as a constitutionally permissible exception. Abe's 2015 reinterpretation allowing collective self-defence without formal constitutional amendment was deeply controversial — reflecting unresolved questions about Japan's wartime responsibility and its role in the postwar order.

terms: Constitution clause renouncing war; allows SDF as 'self-defence' only; contested
Pre-war industrial conglomerates; dissolved during occupation; succeeded by keiretsu
Post-war corporate networks; looser successor to zaibatsu
Ministry of International Trade and Industry; directed industrial policy
1985; G5 agreement appreciating the yen; fuelled asset bubble
1990s stagnation after bubble collapse; sometimes 'Lost Two Decades'
March 11, 2011; Tōhoku earthquake-tsunami and Fukushima nuclear disaster
Abe Shinzō's economic policy: monetary easing, fiscal stimulus, structural reform

quiz.q: Article 9 of Japan's 1947 Constitution states that Japan:
opts: Maintains the emperor as head of state with full executive authority
Renounces war and the maintenance of war potential
Guarantees the right to armed self-defence
Prohibits foreign military bases on Japanese soil
quiz.exp: Article 9 renounces war as a sovereign right and prohibits maintaining war potential. Japan's Self-Defence Forces are justified as a constitutionally permissible exception; Abe's 2015 reinterpretation allowing collective self-defence was highly controversial.

quiz.q: The US-Japan Security Treaty (1951, renewed 1960) contributed to Japan's economic miracle by:
opts: Providing direct American financial aid
Allowing Japan to keep defence spending minimal, freeing resources for industrial investment
Giving Japan access to American military technology for civilian use
Protecting Japanese exports from American tariffs
quiz.exp: Under the American security umbrella, Japan maintained minimal defence spending (typically under 1% of GDP), allowing resources to be channelled into industrial investment and economic development.

quiz.q: Japan's 'Lost Decade' of the 1990s was caused primarily by:
opts: The end of Cold War defence contracts
The collapse of the asset price bubble that had inflated through the late 1980s
A series of trade embargoes imposed by the United States
The sudden death of Prime Minister Miyazawa
quiz.exp: The Plaza Accord (1985) and low interest rates fuelled a massive bubble in stock and real estate prices. When the Bank of Japan raised rates to cool the bubble, it collapsed — leading to bank failures, deflation, and prolonged stagnation.

quiz.q: The 3/11 Tōhoku disaster (2011) combined:
opts: A volcanic eruption, typhoon, and tsunami
An earthquake, tsunami, and nuclear plant meltdowns at Fukushima
A flood, earthquake, and industrial accident
A tsunami and chemical plant explosion
quiz.exp: The March 11, 2011 event comprised a M9.0 earthquake, a devastating tsunami (killing ~19,000), and three reactor meltdowns at the Fukushima Daiichi plant — Japan's worst peacetime crisis since 1945.

quiz.q: Abenomics (from 2012) was based on what the government called 'three arrows,' which included:
opts: Land reform, zaibatsu dissolution, and educational reform
Aggressive monetary easing, fiscal stimulus, and structural economic reforms
Nuclear expansion, trade liberalisation, and military rearmament
Currency devaluation, tariff removal, and privatisation
quiz.exp: Abe's 'three arrows' were: (1) aggressive monetary easing by the Bank of Japan to end deflation; (2) flexible fiscal stimulus; and (3) structural reforms to improve growth potential. Results were mixed, particularly on the third arrow.
